hints: Write the Hess expression for this combustion as enthalpy of reaction equals sum of formation enthalpies of products minus sum for reactants, remembering elements in standard states have zero value.
Substitute the given values with the correct mole ratio for carbon dioxide, then rearrange to isolate the formation enthalpy of P.
walkthrough:
Set up the Hess link between combustion and formation**
Think of formation enthalpies as building every compound from its elements. The combustion enthalpy is the difference between building the products and building the reactants. So $$\Delta H_{comb} = [4\Delta H_f(\text{CO}_2) + \Delta H_f(\text{N}_2)] - [\Delta H_f(\text{P}) + 4\Delta H_f(\text{O}_2)]$$ Remember $\text{N}_2(\text{g})$ and $\text{O}_2(\text{g})$ are elements in their standard states, so their $\Delta H_f = 0$.

Substitute and solve for the unknown**
Put in the numbers, keeping the 4 in front of $\text{CO}_2$: $$-2036 = 4(-384) - \Delta H_f(\text{P})$$ $$-2036 = -1536 - \Delta H_f(\text{P})$$ Rearranging gives $$\Delta H_f(\text{P}) = -1536 + 2036 = +500 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The positive sign makes sense, a compound rich in triple bonds and with nitrogen is very endothermic relative to its elements.

Final answer: $\Delta H_r = \Sigma \Delta H_f(\text{products}) - \Sigma \Delta H_f(\text{reactants})$
$-2036 = 4(-384) - \Delta H_f(\text{P})$
$\Delta H_f \text{ of P} = +500 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Focus on the bond within the $\text{N}_2$ molecule itself and what must happen to that bond before nitrogen can react.
walkthrough:
Picture what must break for reaction**
$\text{N}_2$ is $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$, one sigma plus two pi bonds packed together. For nitrogen atoms to form new bonds to anything else, that triple bond must first be broken or loosened. Because three shared pairs hold the atoms very tightly, the bond enthalpy is extremely large, so breaking it needs a huge energy input and creates a very high activation energy barrier. That is why nitrogen formed in combustion just stays as $\text{N}_2$.
Final answer: Nitrogen contains a very strong $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond which requires a large amount of energy to break, giving a very high activation energy.

hints: Split the phrase into two parts, what every Bronsted-Lowry acid does with a proton, and what the word weak adds about equilibrium.
Think about the position of the dissociation equilibrium in water and whether $\text{H}^+$ is fully released.
walkthrough:
Recall the Bronsted-Lowry picture**
Forget about pH for a moment. In this theory an acid is simply a particle that gives away a proton, $\text{H}^+$, to a base. So ethyne, $\text{HCN}$ and $\text{Q}$ can all lose $\text{H}^+$ to form their conjugate bases.

Add the meaning of weak**
Weak does not mean dilute, it describes extent of reaction. A weak acid only slightly ionises in water: $$\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-$$ Most molecules stay as $\text{HA}$, only a small fraction form $\text{H}^+$, so the equilibrium lies far to the left.

Final answer: A Bronsted-Lowry acid is a proton, $\text{H}^+$, donor.
Weak means partially dissociated in solution, equilibrium lies well to the left.

hints: Recall how a sigma bond differs from a pi bond in terms of head-on versus sideways overlap of atomic orbitals.
Visualise two parallel p orbitals approaching each other side by side and where the shared electron density will then lie.
walkthrough:
Separate sigma from pi**
A sigma bond is end-on overlap along the line joining the nuclei. A pi bond is completely different, it comes from two p orbitals sitting parallel to each other and overlapping side-on, like two clouds merging at the sides.

Sketch and label correctly**
Draw two dumbbell p orbitals side by side with their lobes parallel. Shade the overlap regions above and below the internuclear line to show the electron density is in two lobes, not on the axis. Label the p orbitals and label the resulting shared region as a pi $(\pi)$ bond. In a triple bond there are two such pi overlaps at right angles plus one central sigma bond.

Final answer: A pi bond is formed by sideways overlap of two adjacent parallel p orbitals.
Electron density lies above and below the plane of the sigma bond axis, labelled pi $(\pi)$ orbital.

hints: Compare the displayed structures of P, $\text{N}\equiv\text{C}-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$, and Q, $\text{H}-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$, and list the triple bonds present in both.
Recall the characteristic infrared wavenumber ranges for carbon carbon triple and carbon nitrogen triple stretches from the Data Booklet.
walkthrough:
Find bonds common to both molecules**
Look carefully: P has $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ in the centre and two $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ ends. Q has one $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ and one $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. So both molecules contain the same two types of triple bond, and both will show both stretches.

Match each bond to its IR range**
Triple bonds absorb at high wavenumber because they are strong and stiff. Use the Data Booklet values: $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ appears around $2150-2250 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and nitrile $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ appears around $2200-2250 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. Quote both the range and the bond for each absorption to earn full credit.

Final answer: 1. $2150-2250 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$
2. $2200-2250 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$

hints: Look at the functional group in R that is lost in reaction 1 and consider whether any small molecule is eliminated when the chain forms.
walkthrough:
Recognise the polymerisation type**
R, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCN}$, contains a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond which opens up to join monomers end to end. No atoms are lost and the nitrile group is untouched, the repeat unit is just the opened alkene. That is the hallmark of addition polymerisation.

hints: Identify what happens to a $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ group on heating under reflux with dilute aqueous acid.
walkthrough:
Hydrolyse the side chain, keep the backbone**
Dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(\text{aq})$ heated under reflux fully hydrolyses nitriles to carboxylic acids: $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{-CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NH}_3$. The carbon backbone of the addition polymer does not break. So simply replace every $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ side group in the given polymer with $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$, giving $\text{---CH}_2\text{---CH}(\text{CO}_2\text{H})\text{---}$ as the repeat unit of S.

hints: Count the longest carbon chain in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ and locate the position of the $\text{-NH}_2$ group for IUPAC numbering.
walkthrough:
Name the three carbon amine**
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ has three carbons with the amino group on the end carbon. The IUPAC name numbers to give the functional group the lowest number, so it is propan-1-amine, also accepted as 1-aminopropane. Reaction 3 has reduced both the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ and the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ with $\text{H}_2$ to give this primary amine.

hints: Think about why aqueous ammonia would favour substitution by water to give an alcohol, and what solvent and physical conditions favour amines instead.
walkthrough:
Choose conditions that favour amine formation**
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ to amine is nucleophilic substitution by $\text{NH}_3$. Use excess concentrated ammonia dissolved in ethanol, not water, otherwise water acts as nucleophile and forms an alcohol. Heat in a sealed container under high pressure to keep volatile ammonia in solution and drive substitution to the amine.
Final answer: heat with concentrated ammonia in ethanolic / alcoholic solution in a sealed tube / under high pressure
